flashcards.back_definition: Reducing a device's attack surface before and after deployment: remove or disable what isn't needed, change defaults, apply secure settings and patches.
flashcards.back_example: Disable Telnet, close unused ports, remove the guest account, turn on the host firewall.
flashcards.back_confusion: Every networked device needs hardening, not only servers: printers, phones and cameras too.
flashcards.back_hook: Less to attack, less to lose.

flashcards.front: What is the first hardening step for any new device?
flashcards.back_definition: Change default credentials, since they are identical across every unit of that model and published online.
flashcards.back_example: A new router still using admin/admin can be taken over by anyone on the network.
flashcards.back_confusion: Changing the password is the start, not the whole job.

flashcards.back_definition: A baseline is the approved secure configuration on record. Drift is the gradual unapproved change away from it over time.
flashcards.back_example: A troubleshooting session re-enables SMBv1 and nobody turns it off again.
flashcards.back_confusion: Hardening is not one-time: compare devices to the baseline regularly and fix drift.
flashcards.back_hook: Write down safe, then check you stay there.

flashcards.back_definition: Free, consensus-based hardening guides from the Center for Internet Security, with specific secure settings for operating systems, browsers, cloud services and more.
flashcards.back_example: A CIS Level 1 benchmark for Windows 11 sets password, audit and firewall settings.
flashcards.back_confusion: CIS Controls are a prioritised list of security practices; CIS Benchmarks are detailed per-product settings.
flashcards.back_hook: A recipe book for secure settings.

flashcards.front: Signature-based vs heuristic and behavioural detection?
flashcards.back_definition: Signature-based matches known malware fingerprints: fast and accurate for known threats, blind to new ones. Heuristic and behavioural analysis judge what code looks like or does, so they can catch unknown threats but raise more false positives.
flashcards.back_example: A program that starts encrypting hundreds of files a minute is stopped although it has no known signature.
flashcards.back_confusion: Most endpoint products now combine both.
flashcards.back_hook: Recognise the face vs notice the behaviour.

flashcards.back_definition: Software on one device that controls which network traffic may enter and leave that device.
flashcards.back_example: The laptop blocks inbound file-sharing connections on public Wi-Fi.
flashcards.back_confusion: Antivirus checks code; a firewall checks traffic. You need both.

flashcards.back_definition: An endpoint protection platform prevents threats (antivirus, firewall, device control) from one console. EDR records endpoint activity continuously and gives responders tools to investigate, isolate and fix.
flashcards.back_example: EPP blocks a known bad file; EDR shows how an attacker used PowerShell over three days.
flashcards.back_confusion: Prevention will sometimes fail; detection and response cover what gets through.
flashcards.back_hook: EPP is the lock; EDR is the security camera with a response team.

flashcards.front: What is living off the land?
flashcards.back_definition: Attackers use tools already on the system (PowerShell, WMI, certutil) instead of their own malware, so there is little for signature scanning to find.
flashcards.back_example: certutil.exe used to download a payload from the internet.
flashcards.back_confusion: Behaviour-based detection and logging of command lines catch it better than file scanning.
flashcards.back_hook: No new tools, just your tools used badly.

flashcards.back_definition: A CVE is a unique public ID for a known vulnerability. CVSS is a 0 to 10 severity score for it.
flashcards.back_example: NVD scores CVE-2017-0144 (EternalBlue) 8.8, High, under CVSS v3.1.
flashcards.back_confusion: A high CVSS score is not the whole story: whether it is being exploited and how exposed you are also matter.
flashcards.back_hook: CVE names it; CVSS rates it.

flashcards.back_definition: A zero-day is exploited before any patch exists. An n-day has a patch available that the target has not applied.
flashcards.back_example: WannaCry used an n-day: Microsoft's fix had been out for two months.
flashcards.back_confusion: Most breaches use n-days, not zero-days.
flashcards.back_hook: Zero days of warning vs n days of delay.

flashcards.back_definition: By whether the flaw is being actively exploited (for example, on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list), its severity, and how exposed the affected system is.
flashcards.back_example: An internet-facing VPN with an exploited critical flaw is patched before an internal printer's medium-severity bug.
flashcards.back_confusion: Untested patches can break things, so test, but move fastest on exploited, exposed flaws.

flashcards.back_definition: The time between a vendor releasing a fix and an organisation installing it, when the flaw is public but still open.
flashcards.back_example: Attackers often reverse-engineer a patch within days to build an exploit.
flashcards.back_confusion: Once a patch is public, the clock is running for everyone who hasn't applied it.
flashcards.back_hook: The patch is out; so is the secret.

flashcards.front: What do you do with software that can't be patched?
flashcards.back_definition: Use compensating controls: isolate it on its own network segment, restrict access, monitor it closely, and plan its replacement.
flashcards.back_example: An old lab machine on Windows 7 is kept off the internet and reachable from one admin host.
flashcards.back_confusion: Compensating controls lower risk; they do not fix the flaw.
flashcards.back_hook: If you can't fix it, fence it.
